GPT-6 Astra beat Portal, and it only cost $571.18 The latest model from OpenAl proved its mettle by tackling
Valve's iconic first-person puzzler. User cozyblaze got the Al to beat the full game in under 24 hours for less than $600! And it probably only required a small swimming pool's worth of water to boot. There's a video of a condensed version of the run.

The strongest argument I see for continuing to train much smarter models quickly
is the need to build defensive systems
against the dangers posed by other Al.

Infographic titled "What travels with positive AI sentiment? 1/2 Economic outlook and institutions" featuring four scatter plots analyzing national public sentiment on AI against economic and institutional indicators. Every plot shares a vertical y-axis measuring positive AI sentiment, defined as the percentage of people who agree that AI products and services have more benefits than drawbacks.
 * Prosperity (top-left): Compares AI sentiment against GDP per person PPP (logarithmic x-axis, n=32, r=-0.68). Shows a strong negative correlation, indicating that wealthier nations tend to have lower positive sentiment towards AI.
 * Expectations for the next generation (top-right): Compares AI sentiment against the percentage of people who believe children will be financially better off than their parents (n=28, r=+0.67). Shows a strong positive correlation, indicating that higher optimism for future generations aligns with higher positive AI sentiment.
 * Trust in institutions (bottom-left): Compares AI sentiment against the Edelman Trust Index scale of 0 to 100 (n=24, r=+0.73). Shows a strong positive correlation, indicating higher trust in institutions correlates with higher positive AI sentiment.
 * Concern about inequality (bottom-right): Compares AI sentiment against the percentage of people who view the rich-poor gap as a very big problem (n=28, r=+0.11). Shows virtually no correlation.

Infographic titled "What travels with positive AI sentiment? 2/2 Inequality and attitudes toward AI" featuring four scatter plots analyzing national public sentiment on AI against measures of inequality and self-reported perceptions of AI. Every plot shares a vertical y-axis measuring positive AI sentiment, defined as the percentage of respondents who agree that AI products and services have more benefits than drawbacks.
 * Measured inequality (top-left): Compares AI sentiment against national Gini index values ranging from 0 to 100, where higher indicates greater inequality (World Bank data 2019–2024, n=29). Shows scatter across varied Gini index levels without a single linear pooled trend line.
 * Self-reported AI understanding (top-right): Compares AI sentiment against the percentage of respondents who agree "I have a good understanding of AI" (Ipsos spring 2026, n=32, r=+0.67). Shows a strong positive correlation, indicating that higher self-reported AI understanding aligns with higher positive AI sentiment.
 * Expected job replacement (bottom-left): Compares AI sentiment against the percentage of respondents who believe AI is likely to replace their own job within 5 years (Ipsos spring 2026, n=32, r=+0.90). Shows a very strong positive correlation, where populations higher in expected job replacement also express higher positive AI sentiment.
 * Nervousness about AI (bottom-right): Compares AI sentiment against the percentage of respondents who agree "AI products and services make me nervous" (Ipsos spring 2026, n=32, r=-0.15). Shows a slight negative trend but overall weak correlation.

The study of deep learning-based Al is largely an experimental science. We put a lot of effort into building principled algorithms and making testable predictions, but fundamentally, our large-scale training runs are experiments, and we are sometimes surprised by their results. Moreover, as the systems become more capable, the results become harder to interpret.

Another good rule of thumb: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. We need not just e.g. the counterexample to an outstanding mathematical conjecture, but also all of the inputs that went into finding it.

What data was the system trained on? What were the people running it using it to do? Anything short of that is. not. science.

We aim to safely build an automated Al researcher that can work under human supervision to further progress on deep learning and alignment, enabling iterative improvements. Acconding to our measurements, we have now reached the goal, announced last fall, of having an automated research intern by September of this year. By "research intern," we mean a system that can carry out well-defined research tasks under human direction, including tasks that would take a skilled researcher a few days. We are making strong progress toward creating an automated Al researcher by March of 2028.
